slides.title: Ask the question
slides.lead: Start from the problem — not from the data.
points: Problem: one talk, limited time, many possible topics
Question: what do you actually need to hear most?
Success: your real questions get answered
slides.lesson: A clear question decides what data you need to collect.

slides.title: Collect the data
slides.lead: Designing a form is designing your data.
points: Anonymous, name optional → more honest answers
Multiple choice to count · open text to capture real questions
slides.callout: Reality: the first version had 2 duplicate questions and 1 question that lost all its options — we fixed the form while it was live.
slides.lesson: Always test with a few people before sending it to everyone.

slides.title: Clean the data
slides.lead: Real data is rarely usable as-is.
points: Google Forms joins multiple answers with commas — but the answers themselves contain commas (“Python, SQL, Power BI…”)
→ Splitting on commas fails; match against the original option list instead
40+ open-text ideas → merged into 18 questions in 4 groups
slides.lesson: Most of a data project's time is spent right here.

slides.title: The industry
slides.sub: Career roles, the market, and AI in practice.

slides.title: How do AI, ML, DL and Data Science relate?

defs.d: Machines doing tasks that normally need human intelligence.
A branch of AI: machines learn patterns from data instead of hand-written rules.
A branch of ML: many-layered neural networks — images, speech, language (LLMs).
Getting insight from data with statistics and analysis — using ML/DL when needed.

slides.note: The overlap: Data Science uses ML as a tool — but not all Data Science work is AI.

slides.kicker: What can you do with a Data Science & AI degree?
slides.title: 5 core roles — one flow of data

items.name: ML Engineer
items.q: How does the model run for real?

items.name: AI Engineer
items.q: How do we build AI products?

slides.more: Also: BI Analyst · MLOps Engineer · Research Scientist · Data Product Manager…

slides.name: Data Engineer
slides.tagline: Builds the “pipes” so data arrives correct, complete, and on time.
roadmap: Big data & cloud: Spark, Kafka, AWS/GCP
work: Collect data from many sources: apps, web, sales systems
Clean, standardize, load into the warehouse
Monitor pipelines: fix late, missing, or wrong data

cases.d: Sales data is scattered across stores, web, and app → unify it in one warehouse, refreshed nightly → the whole company shares one revenue number.
A ride-hailing app needs driver locations every second → a streaming pipeline (Kafka) feeds the matching system.

slides.name: Data Analyst
slides.tagline: Turns data into answers to business questions.
work: Take questions from sales and marketing

cases.d: Break it down by region, channel, product → the drop is concentrated in one channel after a delivery-policy change.
Compare 2 versions with a statistical test → ship the one that lifts orders. Today's survey case study is Data Analyst work too.

slides.name: Data Scientist
slides.tagline: Builds models that predict and support decisions.
work: Turn business problems into prediction problems
Prepare data, engineer features, train & evaluate models

cases.d: A telco / app predicts who is about to quit → customer care sends offers to the right people before they leave.
A bank predicts repayment ability from transaction history → faster loan approval, fewer bad debts.

slides.name: ML Engineer
slides.tagline: Takes models from a notebook into a product that runs for real.
roadmap: Strong programming: Python, data structures, Git
work: Package models as fast, stable APIs
Monitor: data shifts → accuracy drops → retrain

cases.d: An e-commerce site shows “you may also like” to millions of users, answering in tens of milliseconds.
Every card transaction is risk-scored by a model right before approval.

slides.name: AI Engineer
slides.tagline: Builds applications on top of AI models — especially LLMs.
work: Connect LLMs to company data and tools
Design RAG and agents; measure answer quality
Optimize cost and latency; control hallucinations

cases.d: Staff ask about processes and policies → a RAG system finds the right document and answers with sources.
Looks up orders, reschedules, files tickets by calling system APIs — not just replying with text.

slides.question: How many hours a day? Can I leave early if I finish early?
quotes: How many hours does an employee work on average? If I finish early, can I go home early?
answer: 8 hours a day, like any normal job.
Whether you can leave early depends on the company — but finishing early does usually mean some free time.

slides.question: How is school knowledge different from work at a company?
quotes: What should students prepare so they aren't caught off guard?
I don't really understand what companies need from me yet.
answer: Companies use far less knowledge than you learn at school.
So learn what's taught at school solidly.

slides.question: Do I need to know many programming languages?
quotes: Does this field require knowing many languages?
slides.stat: 10/29 don't know which tools / languages to learn
answer: Once you master one language, picking up others is easy.
I learned Python, then got “pushed” into PHP, JS, C#, Dart, Kotlin, Swift… and handled them all.

slides.kicker: I only started coding recently — is it too late?
slides.text: Of course not. Everyone has to start somewhere.
slides.sub: What matters most is learning and practicing.

slides.question: How do I learn effectively? What should I avoid?
quotes: Share how you started, how to learn effectively, and what to avoid.
slides.stat: 11/29 don't know how to self-study or find materials
answer: Don't skip the parts that don't make sense to you.
Whenever you feel you don't fully get it, ask questions.

slides.intro: The best material is still papers and books. To get started:

slides.kicker: Does school skip what companies need?
slides.sub: Companies are the ones struggling to apply academic knowledge.

slides.question: Is what I learn at university enough for work?
quotes: Which practical knowledge, skills, or mindsets do companies need that students usually lack?
answer: Real business problems can only be solved with university-level or advanced academic knowledge — not internal experience alone.
Many engineers look down on university knowledge and get stuck. It's most obvious in data & AI.
For now: master the theory in class. You'll understand once you hit real problems.

slides.question: Is building an LLM from scratch feasible?
quotes: Is it feasible to build a large language model from scratch, without relying on any existing model?
slides.lead: Yes — but be clear: building to learn is far easier; building to commercialize takes enormous resources.

slides.question: AI changes constantly — how do I keep up?
quotes: AI never stops changing, so how can we keep up with the trends?
answer: Follow channels and blogs: LinkedIn, Substack, Reddit.
But to understand what you read, you need solid foundations first.
Many buzzwords are hype with little real value — foundations let you question them, and yourself.

slides.kicker: So how should I do personal projects?
slides.text: The more fundamental something is, the longer it lasts.
slides.sub: Focus on understanding what you build and what you learn — more than the result. Technology changes fast; fundamentals stay.

slides.question: How do I grow fast?
quotes: How do I get promoted quickly?
slides.text: At work you'll make mistakes and see your weaknesses → that's when you learn. With the new knowledge, go back and practice to sharpen it. Repeat.
slides.aside_q: “Will AI Engineers be replaced by AI too?”
slides.aside_a: If AI Engineers get replaced by AI, who builds the AI? 🤔

slides.question: Common mistakes when you're new
quotes: What mistakes do fresh graduates commonly make in this field?

items.d: My most frequent mistake. If you don't see a vulnerability, it's very hard to fix once it's exploited.
Add 20% to your original estimate. Estimate too tight and you burn out — in outsourcing you may even owe contract penalties.
Log the main data flows when you code — but don't log too much.
Using AI is great, but you still have to learn. AI output always needs human review.
